summary: Curry County, OR: a 1924 Region 5 cabin on Iron Mountain in the Siskiyou NF, given an L-4 cab in 1940 and gone by 1963; a public trail reaches the summit.

facts.design: Region 5 20'x20' cabin (1924), replaced with an L-4 cab in 1940
facts.status_note: Lookout removed in 1963 per the register; no source describes what remains on the summit
facts.agency: U.S. Forest Service, Siskiyou National Forest

access.note: Reached by the public Iron Mountain Trail, open year round with access limited late fall through spring; no water on the trail

visit.trail_note: Iron Mountain Trail; a short side trail from the ridge leads to the former lookout high point

events.note: Region 5 20'x20' cabin; register and firelookout.com date it to 1924; Forest Lookouts says the lumber was sawn in 1924 and the house finished in summer 1925
Lookout went on duty on the 16th of May and reported one fire
George Valentine named as the lookout man
James Cook, a former lookout, attending a service school at Oregon Caves in June 1933
Region 5 cabin replaced with an L-4 cab (register and firelookout.com)
Fire in the lookout station; after the lookout left, the structure toppled, blazing, over a 150-foot cliff
A new lookout building constructed (Forest Lookouts page only)
Register says removed; firelookout.com says destroyed

notes_for_editor: Record height_m 45.7 (150 ft) appears to be the 150-foot cliff in the 1943 item, not a structure height; no source gives a tower height, so height is omitted and no correction is proposed. A 1942 Coast and Geodetic Survey description in the Forest Lookouts page gives the cabin as 20 feet square and about 17 feet high. Sources disagree on the sequence: register and firelookout.com give an L-4 cab in 1940, while Forest Lookouts gives a new building in 1944 after a 1943 fire; a human should check this. The 1924 build year is also disputed (1925 completion per Forest Lookouts). Removed (register) vs destroyed (firelookout.com) in 1963. The trail page is a Forest Service page last updated June 6, 2025; no source describes the summit's current condition.
